**Temu begins Europe-wide pay-by-bank rollout with TrueLayer**

*Account-to-account payments face their clearest mainstream e-commerce test yet, as one of Europe's highest-traffic discount marketplaces adopts pay-by-bank at scale.*

Temu, the Chinese-owned discount marketplace, is rolling out pay-by-bank across its European operations using TrueLayer's infrastructure. Account-to-account payments have so far gained most traction in niche and subscription use cases; the deployment extends the model into high-volume general merchandise for the first time at this scale.

Temu's sheer transaction volume makes this a meaningful proving ground. The platform consistently ranks among the most-downloaded shopping apps in Europe, and its price-sensitive customer base aligns with the economics of pay-by-bank, where merchants avoid card interchange fees. For TrueLayer, the deal follows its acquisition of a Dutch buy-now-pay-later firm and its recent €23 million raise with Italian state backing, consolidating its position as a leading European pay-by-bank provider.

Consumers accustomed to card checkout may resist bank-initiated payments on a general merchandise platform, and conversion rates, refund handling and the absence of chargeback protections remain live concerns. If Temu's adoption holds, it strengthens the case that account-to-account payments are ready for high-volume, low-margin e-commerce, not just regulated verticals such as gambling and utilities.

**Malaysia's central bank sets phased open finance rollout from 2027**

*The country's largest banks will begin sharing individual customer data from January 2027, adding another major Asian market to the global open finance map.*

Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) has published a regulatory framework for open finance that phases in account data sharing from January 1, 2027. Individual customer data sharing begins first, with SME data following from 2028 and other institution types through 2030. The country's largest banks will be first to comply, with smaller institutions following on a staggered timeline. The framework includes explicit provisions for customers to withdraw consent, addressing a concern that has shaped open banking regimes elsewhere.

Malaysia joins a growing roster of Asian markets, including India, Australia and South Korea, that have moved beyond voluntary open banking initiatives toward mandated data-sharing frameworks. BNM's approach draws on elements of both the EU and UK models, combining regulatory compulsion with phased implementation to manage operational risk.

The Malaysian framework represents a potential export market for European firms with open finance technology and consulting capabilities. It also adds to the evidence that open finance is becoming a global regulatory norm rather than a European exception, reinforcing the case for interoperability standards such as those explored in the BIS's Project Aperta.

**EU's consumer credit directive brings BNPL under full regulation from November 20**

*Interest-free instalment and deferred-payment products lose their regulatory exemption across the bloc, forcing providers including Klarna, PayPal and Scalapay to operate as licensed consumer lenders just days before Black Friday.*

From November 20, the EU's revised Consumer Credit Directive brings buy-now-pay-later products under consumer credit law for the first time. The directive, known as CCD2, removes the exemptions that previously allowed short-term, interest-free credit to operate outside the regulatory perimeter. BNPL providers must now conduct creditworthiness assessments, provide standardised pre-contractual disclosures and grant consumers a 14-day right of withdrawal on the credit agreement.

The practical effects are already visible. Some products are being pulled entirely: Adyen has confirmed that Walley will be discontinued in Denmark and Ratepay's 14-day open invoice offering in Austria will end by the deadline. Klarna is restructuring its EU offerings, issuing new credit agreements and routing subscriptions through reusable credit lines to comply. Laura Schulz, Klarna's director of European public affairs, has said the company already runs credit checks on every purchase.

Implementation is uneven. Italy, Spain and Portugal have not yet transposed the directive into national law, meaning the new requirements will not apply there until local legislation is complete. The Netherlands published its draft implementation late, in April 2025. The directive landing one week before Black Friday sharpens the operational pressure on merchants and providers across markets that have transposed it, particularly Germany, France, Belgium and Sweden.
